'''Jenny Harrison''' is an American mathematician and professor of mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Her research interests include [[geometric analysis]] and the intersection of [[algebra]] and [[geometric measure theory]].

==Education and early career==
Harrison grew up in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, and earned her undergraduate degree from the [[University of Alabama]].<ref name="Selvin2">{{cite journal | url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.261.5119.286 | doi=10.1126/science.261.5119.286 | title=Jenny Harrison Finally Gets Tenure in Math at Berkeley | date=1993 | last1=Selvin | first1=Paul | journal=Science | volume=261 | issue=5119 | page=286 | pmid=17836828 | bibcode=1993Sci...261..286S | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Awarded a [[Marshall Scholarship]], she pursued her graduate studies at the [[University of Warwick]]. While at Warwick, Harrison produced a counterexample to a conjecture of [[Arnaud Denjoy]] (a similar one was discovered independently by [[Charles Fefferman]] and [[William Thurston]]) which was published in the [[Annals of Mathematics]] in 1975.<ref name="annals1975">{{cite journal | last = Harrison| first = Jenny| title =Unsmoothable Diffeomorphisms | journal = Annals of Mathematics | volume = 102 | issue = 1 | pages = 85–94 | year = 1975 | doi = 10.2307/1970975| jstor = 1970975}}</ref> She completed her PhD that same year under the supervision of [[Christopher Zeeman]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=32887}}</ref>

[[Hassler Whitney]] served as Harrison's postdoctoral adviser at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (1975–1976), and she was later a [[List of Miller Research Fellows|Miller Research Fellow]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. She served on the faculty at the [[University of Oxford]] and was a Fellow of [[Somerville College, Oxford|Somerville College]] from 1978 to 1981, before returning to Berkeley as an assistant professor.

In 1986, after being denied tenure at Berkeley, Harrison filed a lawsuit alleging gender discrimination. The case drew national attention within the American academic community.<ref name="Selvin1">{{cite journal | url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.252.5014.1781 | doi=10.1126/science.252.5014.1781 | title=Does the Harrison Case Reveal Sexism in Math? | date=1991 |author1-link=Paul R. Selvin | last1=Selvin | first1=Paul | journal=Science | volume=252 | issue=5014 | pages=1781–1783 | pmid=17753244 | bibcode=1991Sci...252.1781S | url-access=subscription }}</ref> A 1993 settlement led to a new review of her research by an independent panel of seven mathematicians and scientists, who recommended her promotion to full professor.<ref name="NYT1993">{{cite news |last1=Gross |first1=Jane |title=University of California Settles Bias Suit by a Woman Professor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/03/06/us/university-of-california-settles-bias-suit-by-a-woman-professor.html |access-date=2024-05-20 |work=The New York Times |date=March 6, 1993}}</ref>

==Research==
Harrison specializes in [[geometric analysis]]. She developed a theory of [[differential chain]]s, a framework that unifies infinitesimal calculus with the classical theory of the smooth continuum.<ref name="TA">{{cite journal |last1=Harrison |first1=J. |last2=Pugh |first2=H. |title=Topological Aspects of Differential Chains |journal=Journal of Geometric Analysis |date=2012 |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=685–690 |doi=10.1007/s12220-010-9163-x}}</ref> Her work in this area provides methods that apply to domains including [[soap film]]s, [[fractals]], and [[Whitney conditions|Whitney stratified spaces]].<ref name="Hodge2006">{{cite journal |last1=Harrison |first1=Jenny |title=Geometric Hodge star operator with applications to the theorems of Gauss and Green |journal=Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |date=2006 |volume=140 |issue=1 |pages=135–155 |doi=10.1017/S0305004105008716}}</ref>

Her research includes applications to the calculus of variations and continuum mechanics. She has notably worked on [[Plateau's problem]], providing proofs regarding the existence of solutions for boundary curves that account for various soap film structures found in nature.<ref name="Plateau">{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12220-012-9337-x | doi=10.1007/s12220-012-9337-x | title=Soap Film Solutions to Plateau's Problem | date=2014 | last1=Harrison | first1=J. | journal=Journal of Geometric Analysis | volume=24 | pages=271–297 | arxiv=1106.5839 }}</ref> She also extended the [[divergence theorem]] (Gauss–Green theorem) to apply to fractal boundaries.<ref name="Duke1992">{{cite journal |last1=Harrison |first1=Jenny |last2=Norton |first2=Alec |title=The Gauss-Green theorem for fractal boundaries |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |date=1992 |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=575–588 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-92-06725-7}}</ref> This work builds upon and generalizes previous solutions by [[Jesse Douglas]], [[Herbert Federer]], and [[Wendell Fleming]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Federer |first1=Herbert |last2=Fleming |first2=Wendell |title=Normal and integral currents |journal=Annals of Mathematics |date=1960 |volume=72 |issue=3 |pages=458–520 |doi=10.2307/1970225}}</ref>

==Awards and fellowships==
* [[Foundational Questions Institute]] (FQXi) Research Award, 2009
* Miller Professor, [[Miller Institute for Basic Research in Science]], 2007
* Visiting Research Professor, [[Rockefeller University]], 1996–97
* [[National Science Foundation]] Visiting Scholar, [[Yale University]], 1989–90
* CUF Lecturer and Tutorial Fellow, [[Somerville College, Oxford]], 1978–81
* Miller Fellow, [[University of California, Berkeley]], 1977–78
* Visiting Fellow, [[Institute for Advanced Study]], Princeton, 1975–76
